extracted.intended_audience: Catholic educators, university founders, clergy, academics and policymakers concerned with university curriculum
extracted.subtask_description: Normative guidance for designing and assessing university institutions and curricula with respect to the inclusion of Theology and the universality of knowledge, argued from a Catholic/philosophical perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality of University Teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: A University, by its very name, 'should teach universal knowledge.' (Johnson: 'a school where all arts and faculties are taught'; Mosheim: the school of Paris 'was the first to embrace all the arts and sciences, and therefore first became a University.')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues that the defining characteristic of a University is its claim to teach the whole circle of sciences known; therefore an institution calling itself a University should not exclude any major branch of knowledge. Historical definitions and examples (Johnson, Mosheim, Paris) are offered to justify calling universality a core requirement. If certain branches are excluded, the institution fails to live up to its name and purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of Theology as a Legitimate Branch
rubrics_metrics.description: Theology is 'surely a branch of knowledge' and therefore belongs among the subjects taught at a University. Excluding the subject of Religion from a University implies either that religion is barren of real knowledge or that the institution omits a special and important branch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author frames a syllogism: if a University professes universal knowledge and Theology is a branch of knowledge, Theology must be taught. If an institution excludes Theology, it must either deny that anything is known about God or concede that it omits an important intellectual domain. This is an evaluative test of institutional completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do Not Sacrifice Knowledge in Institutional Compromise
rubrics_metrics.description: Compromise among diverse parties is acceptable, but 'one thing they may not sacrifice—Knowledge itself.' Compromises are permissible only when they do not compromise the main object of the institution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When forming coalitions or joint institutions, participants can give up private opinions and minor differences, but must not abandon the core object (the pursuit and teaching of knowledge). Examples: circulating a common Bible is acceptable, but inserting doctrinal tracts that compromise the committee's principle would be objectionable. The test for legitimacy of compromise is whether the core intellectual object is preserved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency between Name/Aim and Practice
rubrics_metrics.description: It is logically inconsistent for a seat of learning to call itself a University and to exclude the study of Religion; 'such an Institution cannot be what it professes, if there be a God.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions should align their professed aims with their curriculum. If a body claims to teach 'all knowledge' but omits what others rightly consider central knowledge (here Theology), that omission is an internal contradiction and undermines institutional integrity. Evaluations should check for this consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Against Artificial Compartmentalization of Knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: You cannot coherently limit University knowledge to a single 'line' or 'sphere' (senses, intuition, testimony, abstract reasoning) and thereby exclude the science of Religion: religious truths are reported by testimony, history, induction, metaphysical necessity and thus intersect other domains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author rejects the move to exclude Theology by redefining the University's 'line' of inquiry. Evaluators/designers should recognize that religious claims interact with history, metaphysics, ethics and natural theology; therefore exclusion on the basis of a narrow epistemic boundary is philosophically unsound. Use examples given (testimony, history, metaphysical inference) to argue for integration rather than compartmentalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious Truths Treated as Academic Facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Religious propositions (e.g., the Incarnation, existence of angels, eschatological claims) are of the same nature as historical or metaphysical facts and thus merit academic consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text treats certain theological claims as historical/metaphysical matters comparable to scientific or historical facts. Curriculum designers and assessors should therefore consider theological propositions as legitimate objects of scholarly study, on par with other factual subject-matter, and provide appropriate methods and forums for their examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical Expediency Permits Temporary 'Second-Best' Arrangements
rubrics_metrics.description: Where no direct duty forbids, it may be necessary under particular circumstances to accept arrangements that are 'abstractedly best' only in theory; 'a system of what is called secular Education...may, in a particular place or time, be the least of evils.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author concedes that practical constraints (political, social, economic) can justify temporary or local departures from the ideal university model. Evaluations should therefore be context-sensitive: judge whether secular or mixed arrangements are pragmatic, temporary, and administered in ways that minimize harms and allow later improvement toward the ideal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use External Expertise Regardless of Confessional Source
rubrics_metrics.description: There is reason 'for availing ourselves of the investigations and experience of those who are not Catholics' when addressing Liberal Education; the Church has historically made use of external witnesses and authorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance: when developing curricula or policies, it is legitimate and often beneficial to consult and adopt findings, methods, or materials from non-Catholic scholars and institutions. The author cites historical precedent (use of Protestant scholars by Catholic editors, Benedict XIV citing Protestants) to normalize borrowing where it advances education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deference to Ecclesiastical Authority for Catholics
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Ecclesiastical authority, not argument, is the supreme rule and the appropriate guide for Catholics in matters of religion. It has lately exercised it in our own instance: it has interposed in favour of a pure University system for Catholic youth, forbidding compromise or accommodation of any kind.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For Catholic stakeholders, ecclesiastical decisions about the structure and nature of Catholic universities carry binding moral and institutional weight. Even when arguing on grounds of reason, Catholics should accept and obey authoritative ecclesiastical rulings; such decisions also function as practical endorsements of expediency and trustworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate Belief-conception When Assessing Institutional Choices
rubrics_metrics.description: If religion is regarded as feeling or sentiment rather than knowledge, then exclusion of Theology from a University follows coherently; conversely, if religion is regarded as knowledge, exclusion is incoherent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing why an institution excludes religion, examine the underlying conception of religion (knowledge vs. feeling). Institutional choices should be evaluated for internal consistency: an institution that professes to teach knowledge but treats religion as mere sentiment is being philosophically inconsistent; evaluators should make this presupposition explicit and critique accordingly.
